tagline.text: A Cebu heritage city where old mansions and the scent of chicharon linger

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half day to a full day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 per person (day trip from Cebu City)

children.text: About 40km south of Cebu City, Carcar is one of Cebu's oldest towns, established as a settlement in 1599. A white St. Catherine Church and Spanish- and American-era mansions cluster around its plaza, and crispy chicharon and lechon have made it a favorite lunch stop on southern Cebu trips.
Carcar lies on the southeastern coast of Cebu Island, about
40km
from Cebu City along the southern coastal road. Before the Spanish arrived, it was a village called Kabkad; the Augustinians established the parish and formal settlement in
. It's one of Cebu's oldest towns, with over 300 years of Spanish rule behind it, and was raised to city status in
. To Cebuanos, it's known as a heritage city and the home of chicharon and lechon.

The heart of the city is the hilltop plaza. St. Catherine Church, built of coral stone in the 19th century, looks down over the plaza, surrounded by the Carcar City Museum (converted from an old clinic), school and convent buildings, and the Rizal monument. A short walk from the plaza brings you to a row of houses built by families who made their fortunes in sugar and trade, including Balay Na Tisa (the Sarmiento-Osmeña House), a tiled-roof house built in
, the Mediterranean-blue Mercado Mansion, and the sprawling Noel family residence, Dakong Balay.
Carcar also carved out a place in World War II history. In
April 1944

, fishermen from this town recovered a box that had drifted ashore from a Japanese plane downed at sea; the documents inside, later known as the Koga Papers, detailed Japanese naval operational plans. Passed through guerrillas and a U.S. submarine to the Allies, the documents are said to have provided an important clue for planning the liberation of the Philippines.

This is a place best enjoyed slowly — small streets, old houses, and market food rather than one big sight — so it suits travelers interested in history and architecture, and those who love to eat. Lying on the route to Simala Shrine, Oslob, and Moalboal, the most common way to visit is a
2–3 hour
stop in the middle of a southern Cebu itinerary.
A striking church with white walls, twin bell towers, and a row of white saints' statues lining the churchyard. Inside, a rose-motif ceiling painting by Cebuano artist Canuto Avila from the
catches the eye. Blending Mudejar and Baroque styles, it carries a National Historical Commission marker.

In front of the church, the plaza brings together the Carcar City Museum (converted from an old clinic), the Rizal monument, and old school buildings. Sit on a bench under the trees and take in this layered scene of Spanish- and American-era history at a leisurely pace.

blocks.title: Balay Na Tisa and the Old Mansion Lane

children.text: Balay Na Tisa, Cebuano for "tiled-roof house," was built in
and ranks among Cebu's oldest homes. Nearby, the Mercado Mansion and Dakong Balay are mostly privately owned, so admire them from the outside, and step inside only during posted open hours.

A circular monument stands where the southern coastal road forks at the town's entrance, made by Carcar-born sculptor Ramon Abellana based on a sketch by his brother, Martino Abellana. It's the landmark that tells you you've arrived in Carcar.

Carcar chicharon, deep-fried pork rind with a bit of meat attached, is crispy and a signature souvenir Cebuanos love to bring home. Try it fresh from shops around the rotunda and public market, dipped in vinegar sauce.

blocks.title: Lechon Lunch at the Public Market

children.text: Inside the market, lechon stalls carve up whole roast pigs on the spot and sell them by weight. The local way to eat is Cebu-style lechon, crispy-skinned and lemongrass-scented inside, paired with puso (rice steamed in woven coconut-leaf pouches).
Carcar is known as Cebu's "shoe capital" for its many handmade-shoe workshops. Browsing shops selling inexpensive leather sandals and shoes around town is a small pleasure of its own.
Old-fashioned treats like ampao, puffed rice bound with syrup, and bocarillo, shredded coconut simmered in sugar, are also Carcar specialties. Light and long-lasting, they make good gifts.

Simala Shrine is about
20–30 minutes
south of Carcar, so the two pair well. If you're heading down to Oslob or Moalboal, use Carcar as a lunch stop along the way.

4 hours 30 minutes to 5 hours

1 hour 20 minutes
from Manila.
From the airport to Carcar is about
50km

1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours
by car. Taking the southern coastal expressway (via the CCLEX bridge and coastal road) around Cebu City can help you avoid some downtown congestion.
Ceres buses toward Sibonga, Argao, Oslob, and Moalboal from Cebu City South Bus Terminal (CSBT) nearly all pass through Carcar. It takes about
1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes

and are a bit faster.

It's about
10–15 minutes
on foot from the rotunda up to the hilltop plaza, but the uphill walk is easier by tricycle (about
). The plaza and old mansion lane are easy to explore entirely on foot.
Southern Cebu is dry during
December–May
, good for exploring the town on foot.
January to March
is relatively cool with clear skies, ideal for photos of the white church. In
April and May
, midday temperatures climb to
, so walk in the morning and late afternoon, and rest inside the church or a restaurant at midday. During the
June–November
rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent, and southern roads can back up when a typhoon passes.
Around the feast of the city's patron saint, St. Catherine (
November 25
), the Kabkaban Festival runs from
November 23 to 25

with street parades, live music, and religious processions filling the city. Traffic is restricted and lodging fills up quickly during this period. Holy Week brings church events worth seeing, but some sites, like the museum, may close, so check their status beforehand.

Carcar is mostly a day-trip stop, so lodging options are limited. Downtown has simple inns and guesthouses at about

a night; for more comfort, stay in Cebu City or Mactan and visit as a day trip. If you're heading down to Oslob or Moalboal, use Carcar as a lunch stop and stay overnight in a southern beach town instead.

Carcar's real pleasure is its food. Lechon stalls cluster around the public market and rotunda, letting you pick out the exact cuts of freshly roasted whole pig you want, and chicharon shops offer a range from thick, meaty pieces to chicharon bulaklak made from fried intestines. Market eateries serve lechon, fish soup, and grilled dishes with puso at low prices. For dessert or a gift, try ampao (puffed rice candy), bocarillo (coconut candy), and the glutinous-rice treat gorgoritas.
Visit the church quietly when Mass isn't in session. Covering your shoulders and knees is considered proper etiquette, and please refrain from photography during Mass.
Most of the old mansions are privately owned and lived in. Don't enter through the gate without permission — visit only the houses that are open, following their posted guidelines.
Lechon is freshest from late morning through lunchtime. Popular stalls sometimes sell out by early afternoon.
Freshly fried chicharon stays crispy for days. If you're taking it home on a flight, pack it in a sturdy bag or box so it doesn't crumble.
Buses stop along the road in front of the rotunda. To head back, just flag down a Cebu City-bound bus near the rotunda.
Many market stalls and street vendors accept cash only. Bring plenty of small bills.
If you have extra time, it's worth stopping to relax at the Guadalupe Mabugnao Mainit hot spring on the outskirts of town. Confirm the route and operating status locally.

Beside the road in Barangay Valladolid, north of the town center, stands the old Carcar station building of the Cebu Railway, which linked Danao and Argao in the early 20th century. It is a heritage building no longer in use, so you can't go inside, and since it's a roadside with heavy truck traffic, just stop briefly at the roadside for a photo and move on.
The southern coastal road around the rotunda carries heavy bus and truck traffic. Don't step onto the road for photos — use the crosswalk.
Walking around at midday in the heat can be intense. Bring water and a hat, and rest in the shade often.
The market interior is crowded and the floors can be wet and slippery. Wear your bag in front and keep an eye on your belongings.
During the Kabkaban Festival and Holy Week, road closures and heavy traffic are common, so allow extra travel time.
The route back to Cebu City in the late afternoon can be badly congested around Talisay and Minglanilla, taking
2 hours
or more.
During heavy rain from Tropical Depression Verbena on
November 25, 2025

, rivers overflowed, flooding Poblacion 1, 2, and 3 barangays up to knee height, and water also entered the basement of Balay na Tisa. If heavy rain is forecast in the rainy season, postpone your visit and check flood advisories for low-lying roads.
